## The problem {#sec-housing-brief}

::: {.callout-note}
## About this specification
This project was the final assignment of the machine-learning course of the
master I attended. The specification below is **my own restatement** of the
requirements, written for this handbook; it does not reproduce the course
material.
:::

**Context.** A company that estimates residential property prices uses a
multiple linear regression built in a hurry some time ago. On the sales it was
fitted on it looks fine, but on properties it has not seen its errors are
larger than expected. The suspicion is **overfitting**, and the question is
whether **regularisation** would help — and, along the way, which
characteristics of a property really drive its estimated price, something the
company needs in order to explain its valuations to clients.

**What the analysis must do.**

- **R1 — Data.** Start from a public data set of residential sales with the
  price (the target) and a dozen characteristics: lot area, numbers of
  bedrooms, bathrooms, storeys and parking places, six yes/no amenities, and
  a furnishing status with three levels.
- **R2 — Exploration first.** Inspect types, distributions and missing values,
  and build the correlation matrix of the numerical features with the price.
- **R3 — Justified preprocessing.** Decide how to treat missing values
  (deletion or imputation, and why), encode the categorical variables with the
  appropriate method (ordinal where an order exists, one-hot where it does
  not), and scale the numerical features — essential with penalised models.
- **R4 — A baseline.** Fit an unregularised multiple linear regression and
  measure it on training and test data (hold-out); a large gap would be
  concrete evidence of overfitting.
- **R5 — Three regularised models**: ridge, lasso and elastic net.
- **R6 — One comparison protocol.** Compare the models with **k-fold
  cross-validation**, not a single split; for each model, try several values
  of the penalty and report how the error and the coefficients change.
- **R7 — Comparable metrics.** Mean squared error for every model on the same
  validation scheme, with the coefficient of determination alongside;
  comment on the order of magnitude of the MSE, which depends on the units of
  the price.
- **R8 — Coefficients, not only errors.** For each model, count the
  coefficients that remain non-zero and list the largest in absolute value;
  explain how the three methods differ and what that means for interpreting
  the market.
- **R9 — Charts that support decisions**: the errors of the models side by
  side, the error as a function of the penalty, a learning curve, and the
  residuals (against predicted values, and their distribution) — checking
  whether the model errs systematically on some price bands.
- **R10 — Readable by non-programmers.** A notebook alternating code and
  explanation (what was done, why, what was observed), ending with
  conclusions and an operational recommendation: which model, under which
  conditions.
- **R11 — Method with AI assistants.** If an assistant is used, give it
  specific prompts (data, goal, output format) and verify its code — in
  particular that preprocessing does not leak into validation and that the
  metrics are the requested ones.

**What counts as quality.** Not the final error figure, but a fair,
documented comparison: motivated preprocessing, sound validation, and careful
reading of coefficients and residuals.

## The data and their provenance {#sec-housing-data}

The brief points to a CSV file of 545 sales. Before using — and citing — a
data set, find out where it comes from. Three facts, all checked in code
below:

1. The course's file is a re-encoding of the Kaggle **"Housing Prices
   Dataset"** by M Yasser H [@yasser2021], released on Kaggle under **CC0**
   (public domain). The Kaggle file stores the yes/no columns as text; the
   course's copy stores them as 1/0 and the furnishing status as integers. The
   handbook uses an identical copy of the Kaggle file (`ml/_data/housing.csv`).
2. The Kaggle file is in turn derived from the sample of **546 houses sold in
   Windsor, Ontario (Canada), in 1987** studied by Anglin and Gençay
   [@anglin1996], whose data are in the *Journal of Applied Econometrics* data
   archive [@anglin1996data] and in the R package Ecdat [@croissant2025]. Every
   one of the 545 Kaggle rows matches one of the 546 original sales exactly,
   once the Kaggle price is divided by **70**; one sale is missing; the
   columns were **renamed**; and a `furnishingstatus` column that does **not**
   exist in the original study was added, with no documentation of its origin.
3. The course's integer coding of furnishing is furnished = 1,
   semi-furnished = 2, unfurnished = 0 — not the natural order. This is the
   only coding that reproduces the correlations and results printed in the
   reviewed notebook (@sec-housing-replay).

The renaming matters for interpretation, because some new names say more than
the original variables did:

| Kaggle / course name | Original variable [@anglin1996; @croissant2025] |
|---|---|
| `price` | sale price in Canadian dollars of 1987 (× 70 in the Kaggle file) |
| `area` | **lot size** in square feet — not the floor area of the house |
| `bedrooms`, `bathrooms`, `stories` | numbers of bedrooms, full bathrooms, storeys (excluding the basement) |
| `mainroad` | the house has a **driveway** |
| `guestroom` | the house has a **recreational room** |
| `basement` | the house has a **full finished** basement |
| `hotwaterheating` | the house uses **gas for hot-water heating** |
| `airconditioning` | central air conditioning |
| `parking` | number of **garage** places |
| `prefarea` | located in the preferred neighbourhood of the city |
| `furnishingstatus` | *not in the original data; origin undocumented* |

: What the columns of the house data really measure {#tbl-housing-columns}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the provenance check"
import hashlib
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from collections import Counter

kaggle = mlbook.load_housing()
print("MD5 of the handbook's copy:", hashlib.md5((mlbook.DATA / "housing.csv").read_bytes()).hexdigest())

# The Anglin–Gençay sample as distributed by the R package Ecdat (CSV copy from Rdatasets, pinned commit)
ECDAT = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vincentarelbundock/Rdatasets/"
         "1dcc2bf5f955cc1224a3e1307256e1fe86b68dae/csv/Ecdat/Housing.csv")
windsor = pd.read_csv(ECDAT).drop(columns="rownames")
rename = {"lotsize": "area", "bathrms": "bathrooms", "driveway": "mainroad", "recroom": "guestroom",
          "fullbase": "basement", "gashw": "hotwaterheating", "airco": "airconditioning", "garagepl": "parking"}
windsor = windsor.rename(columns=rename)
cols = ["price", "area", "bedrooms", "bathrooms", "stories", "mainroad", "guestroom", "basement",
        "hotwaterheating", "airconditioning", "parking", "prefarea"]
print("original sample:", windsor.shape, "| Kaggle file:", kaggle.shape)
print("every Kaggle price divisible by 70:", bool((kaggle["price"] % 70 == 0).all()))

k_rows = Counter(map(tuple, kaggle[cols].assign(price=kaggle["price"] // 70).astype(str).to_numpy()))
w_rows = Counter(map(tuple, windsor[cols].astype(str).to_numpy()))
print("Kaggle rows found in the original (price / 70):", sum((k_rows & w_rows).values()), "of", len(kaggle))
print("original sale missing from the Kaggle file:", list(w_rows - k_rows))
print("furnishingstatus in the original data:", "furnishingstatus" in windsor.columns)
```

Two consequences for the project. The data describe **one city in one year,
1987**: a model fitted on them says nothing about prices today, and the
brief's "larger errors on new properties" could come from a changed market as
much as from overfitting. And the `furnishingstatus` column has no documented
origin; the reference implementation therefore also checks how much the
results depend on it (@sec-housing-sensitivity).

## Walkthrough of the published implementation {#sec-housing-walkthrough}

The notebook in `ai-projects` (English version; the Italian original is in the
`it/` folder) has 24 cells — 19 of code — organised as follows.

**Setup and data.** After a short introduction to the business problem, the
imports (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, seaborn, Matplotlib, SciPy) and the
data are loaded from the course's URL. `df.shape` gives 545 × 13 and
`df.isna().sum()` shows **no missing values**; a comment notes that the
categorical variables are already encoded as integers. The full correlation
matrix is printed.

**Preparation.** A seed (`random_seed = 42`) is fixed. The furnishing status is
**one-hot encoded** with `pd.get_dummies(..., drop_first=True)`, with the
comment that its codes 0, 1, 2 should not be treated as weights. The price
distribution is examined: skewness 1.21, reduced to 0.14 by
`np.log1p`, with two histograms; the comment motivates the log transform with
the need for "normal distributions" for these models. The target is then
transformed (`y = np.log1p(y)`), the data split 70/30, and a `StandardScaler`
**fitted on the training part only** and applied to both parts.

**Models.** Two helper functions print the MSE, the $R^2$ and the number of
non-zero coefficients of a fitted model. A loop over
`alpha_params = (0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10)` fits `Ridge`, `Lasso` and
`ElasticNet(l1_ratio=0.5)` and prints their metrics on training and test
data. The comments observe that ridge is stable across $\alpha$, while lasso
and elastic net "drop sharply" from $\alpha = 0.01$ and start zeroing features,
and that there is no overfitting because train and test $R^2$ are close. A
**5-fold cross-validation** is then written by hand for ridge — re-fitting the
scaler inside each fold — and prints mean train and test $R^2$ for each
$\alpha$ (0.699 and 0.666–0.667). Two figures show the test $R^2$ of the three
models against $\alpha$ and the coefficient paths.

**Diagnostics and conclusions.** For `Ridge(alpha=0.1)` the residuals are
plotted against the predicted values and as a histogram; the three largest
coefficients (area, air conditioning, bathrooms) are printed. The concluding
text cell reports a ceiling of $R^2 \approx 0.65$, no overfitting but
"structural underfitting", lasso useful for identifying strong features,
ridge stable, elastic net similar, and recommends to the agency to focus on
amenities such as air conditioning.

**What it does well.** A fixed seed; an explicit missing-value check;
**one-hot encoding of the furnishing status** instead of trusting its integer
codes (the right call: @sec-housing-sensitivity shows that the natural-order
ordinal coding fits worse); a skewness check before transforming the target;
a scaler fitted on training data only — also **inside each fold** of the
hand-written cross-validation, which many published analyses get wrong
(@sec-leakage); the count of non-zero coefficients the brief asks for;
coefficient-path plots; residuals plotted against **predicted** values (the
correct diagnostic, @sec-housing-residuals); and a conclusion that correctly
identifies the key fact — the train/test gap is small, so overfitting is not
the problem.

### Re-executing the notebook {#sec-housing-replay}

Several printed numbers looked surprising: test MSEs of order $10^{-4}$, when
the variance of $\ln(\text{price})$ is about $0.14$; and a lasso that loses
all but two features at $\alpha = 0.01$, although @prp-lambda-max predicts
that on log-prices nothing should vanish before $\alpha \approx 0.2$. The only
way to settle such questions is to **run the code again**. The cell below
downloads the notebook from `ai-projects` (pinned to a commit), rebuilds the
course's CSV from the Kaggle copy (coding furnishing as in fact 3 of
@sec-housing-data), and executes the notebook's code cells in a fresh
namespace — first **from top to bottom**, then in the order recorded by the
execution counters that Jupyter stores in the notebook file.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the replay code"
import io, re, json, contextlib, tempfile, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

NB_URL = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-projects/"
          "2e2c86df3608ff91868a3688c5d3a1d6437a0843/Real_Estate_Price_Forecasting.ipynb")
nb = json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(NB_URL, timeout=60).read())
cells = {i: c for i, c in enumerate(nb["cells"]) if c["cell_type"] == "code"}
code = {i: "".join(c["source"]) for i, c in cells.items()}
published = {i: "".join("".join(o.get("text", "")) for o in c.get("outputs", [])) for i, c in cells.items()}
counts = {i: c.get("execution_count") for i, c in cells.items()}

course_csv = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "housing_course.csv"
mlbook.load_housing(encoded=True).to_csv(course_csv, index=False)

def replay(order):
    """Execute the notebook's code cells in the given order; return each cell's printed output and the namespace."""
    ns, out = {}, {}
    for i in order:
        src = (code[i].replace("https://proai-datasets.s3.eu-west-3.amazonaws.com/housing.csv", str(course_csv))
                      .replace("drop(columns= 'price', axis = 1)", "drop(columns='price')")   # pandas 3 (review item 12)
                      .replace("plt.show()", "plt.close('all')"))
        buf = io.StringIO()
        try:
            with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
                exec(src, ns)
        except Exception as err:
            buf.write(f"[{type(err).__name__}: {err}]")
        out[i] = buf.getvalue()
    return out, ns

def parse_models(text):
    """The table printed by the notebook's model loop (cell 16)."""
    pat = (r"(RIDGE|LASSO|ELASTIC NET) MODEL with alpha =([\d.]+)\nTRAIN\nMSE: ([\d.e-]+)\nR2: ([-\d.e]+)\n"
           r"Model with: (\d+) active.*?\nTEST\nMSE: ([\d.e-]+)\nR2: ([-\d.e]+)")
    df = pd.DataFrame(re.findall(pat, text), columns=["model", "alpha", "train MSE", "train R2", "active", "test MSE", "test R2"])
    return df.astype({"alpha": float, "train MSE": float, "train R2": float, "active": int, "test MSE": float, "test R2": float})

top_down, ns_top = replay(sorted(code))
print("execution counters stored in the notebook (cell: counter):",
      {i: counts[i] for i in sorted(counts, key=lambda i: counts[i])})
```

The counters show that the cells were **not** run from top to bottom: the
seed (cell 8) got counter 12, after the cells around it; the model loop
(cell 16) got 46, after the cross-validation (39) and the plots (34, 38);
counters 10 and 11 are missing — runs of cells whose counters were later
overwritten by re-runs. One hypothesis explains everything: the cell that
transforms the target and splits the data (cell 11) was first run **before**
the seed existed. It executed `y = np.log1p(y)` and then failed on the
undefined `random_seed`; after the seed cell was run, cell 11 was run again —
applying the logarithm a **second** time. Replaying in counter order with
that one extra run:

```{python}
order = [i for i in sorted(counts, key=lambda i: counts[i])]
hypothesis = order.copy()
hypothesis.insert(hypothesis.index(8), 11)          # cell 11 once before the seed: log applied, then NameError
by_counter, ns_hyp = replay(hypothesis)

pub, top, hyp = (parse_models(t[16]) for t in (published, top_down, by_counter))
nums = ["train MSE", "train R2", "test MSE", "test R2"]
print("model loop, largest |published - replay| over all 15 rows x 4 metrics:")
print(f"  replay in counter order + hypothesis: {np.abs(pub[nums].to_numpy() - hyp[nums].to_numpy()).max():.1e}")
print(f"  replay from top to bottom:            {np.abs(pub[nums].to_numpy() - top[nums].to_numpy()).max():.1e}")
print("cross-validation cell, published vs hypothesis replay identical:", published[17].strip() == by_counter[17].strip())
print(f"variance of the target in the published run: {np.var(ns_hyp['y']):.5f} "
      f"(ln(price): {np.var(np.log(mlbook.load_housing()['price'])):.5f})")
print("rows in the 'training set' used by the published model loop:", ns_hyp["x_train"].shape[0],
      "(the 70/30 split has", round(0.7 * 545), "rows)")
```

Every number printed by the published model loop is reproduced to the last
digit (differences of order $10^{-16}$, floating-point noise), and so is the
cross-validation output. The forensic reconstruction yields three findings:

1. **The target was transformed twice**: the published results model
   $\ln(1 + \ln(1 + \text{price}))$, a variable with variance about $0.0005$.
   That is why the MSEs are of order $10^{-4}$.
2. **The lasso and elastic-net "collapse" is an artefact of that scale.** By
   @prp-lambda-max the lasso keeps any feature only while $\alpha <
   \operatorname{sd}(y)\max_j|r_j|$; with the doubly logged target this
   threshold is about $0.0226 \times 0.54 \approx 0.012$, so $\alpha = 0.01$
   already leaves only two features and larger values none. Ridge's penalty
   does not scale with the target (@prp-penalty-scale), so ridge looked
   "stable". On the correctly transformed target nothing collapses (table
   below).
3. **The "hold-out" metrics are not hold-out metrics.** The model loop was last
   run *after* the hand-written cross-validation, which reuses the names
   `x_train`, `x_test`: the printed TRAIN/TEST figures, the $R^2$-vs-$\alpha$
   plot, the residual plots and the top-three coefficients all come from the
   **last fold** of the cross-validation (436/109 rows), not from the 70/30
   split.

Run from top to bottom, the same code gives the results the analysis was meant
to produce:

```{python}
compare = pd.DataFrame({
    "model": pub["model"], "alpha": pub["alpha"],
    "active (published)": pub["active"], "test R2 (published)": pub["test R2"].round(3),
    "active (top to bottom)": top["active"], "test R2 (top to bottom)": top["test R2"].round(3),
    "test MSE (top to bottom)": top["test MSE"].round(4)})
compare
```

On the log-price target, lasso and elastic net keep all 13 coefficients up to
$\alpha = 0.01$ and perform close to ridge; at $\alpha = 0.1$ they start
removing features — a penalty already too strong for these data — and at
$\alpha \ge 1$ (above $\lambda_{\max} \approx 0.2$) they remove all of
them. The grid simply spans the wrong range for the lasso, whatever the
scale of the target (review item 2). The conclusions "Ridge
gave the best results" and "Lasso and Elastic Net collapse" do not survive;
"no overfitting" does.

::: {.callout-important}
## The lesson: restart and run all
A notebook stores the outputs of whatever was executed, in whatever order. A
large study of notebooks on GitHub re-executed 863 878 of them: about 24% ran
without errors and about 4% reproduced their stored results
[@pimentel2019]. Before sharing a notebook: **Kernel → Restart & Run All**,
then read the outputs again. And write cells that can be re-run safely: never
overwrite a variable with a function of itself (`y = np.log1p(y)`); create a
new name (`y_log = np.log(y)`), so that running the cell twice does the same
thing as running it once.
:::

### Code review: refinements suggested by this book {#sec-housing-review}

| # | Observation | Why it matters | Suggested change | Chapter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cells executed out of order; the target was log-transformed twice | all published metrics refer to $\ln(1+\ln(1+\text{price}))$ | Restart & Run All before publishing; idempotent cells (`y_log = ...`) | @sec-housing-replay |
| 2 | One $\alpha$ grid (0.001–10) for ridge, lasso and elastic net | the three penalties are scaled differently; the lasso's useful range depends on the target's scale | a separate grid per model; for lasso/EN anchored at $\lambda_{\max}$ | @tbl-sklearn-penalties, @prp-lambda-max |
| 3 | No unregularised baseline (`LinearRegression` is imported but never used) | the brief's starting point; without it "does regularisation help?" cannot be answered | fit OLS with the same protocol | @sec-multiple-regression |
| 4 | Cross-validation only for ridge, and only $R^2$ | lasso and elastic net are compared on one split; the MSE the brief asks for is never cross-validated | the same repeated k-fold for every model, MSE and $R^2$ | @sec-cross-validation |
| 5 | Conclusions drawn from one split | on these data one split's test $R^2$ ranges from about 0.50 to 0.77 | repeated k-fold; report mean ± standard error | @fig-holdout-variability |
| 6 | The final model is chosen by its test-set score | selection on the test set makes the reported score optimistic | choose $\alpha$ by CV on the training set; test once; nested CV for the comparison | @sec-selection |
| 7 | MSE reported on the transformed scale without units | the brief asks to comment on the magnitude; $10^{-4}$ means nothing to a client | report RMSE on the log scale (≈ relative error) and errors in price units after back-transformation | @sec-housing-test |
| 8 | Log transform justified by "normality" of the target | the Gaussian assumption concerns the errors, not the target; the real reasons are multiplicative effects, relative errors and less heteroscedasticity | justify by relative errors; `np.log` suffices (prices are large) | @thm-ls-mle, @sec-describing |
| 9 | Correlation matrix includes `furnishingstatus` as an integer | its codes (furnished = 1, semi = 2, unfurnished = 0) are not even ordered | exclude it, or correlate its one-hot columns | @sec-variable-types |
| 10 | Business conclusion: add air conditioning and amenities to raise the value | a regression coefficient is an association, not the effect of an intervention; and `area` is the **lot**, not the floor area | phrase as associations; read @tbl-housing-columns | @thm-fwl, @sec-correlation |
| 11 | Conclusion claims both "roughly normal" and "structured" residuals; no learning curve; residuals not examined by price band | the brief asks for both; the claims are not supported by a figure | learning curve; residuals by band of predicted and of actual price | @sec-housing-residuals |
| 12 | `df.drop(columns='price', axis=1)` | raises an error in pandas 3 | `df.drop(columns="price")` | @sec-pandas |
| 13 | `random_state` passed to `Ridge`/`Lasso` | has no effect with the default solvers; suggests randomness that is not there | omit it | — |
| 14 | Manual preprocessing (dummies before the split, scaler per fold by hand) | correct here, but easy to break when the code changes | `ColumnTransformer` + `Pipeline` inside every CV | @sec-leakage |
| 15 | Narrative mostly in code comments | the brief asks for text cells readable by non-programmers | Markdown cells: what, why, what we observed | @sec-housing-conclusions |

: Code review of the published implementation {#tbl-housing-review}

None of these items reflects a misunderstanding of the method: the
preprocessing choices and the main conclusion (no overfitting) are right. Most
of the review — items 1 to 7 — is about the **evaluation protocol**, which is
exactly where the brief puts the value of the work, and item 1 shows how a
notebook can silently drift away from its own code.

## Reference implementation {#sec-housing-reference}

The code below follows the brief step by step. In a notebook each block would
be one cell, preceded by a text cell explaining it (requirement R10); here the
explanations are the surrounding paragraphs.

### Setup, split and preprocessing

The test set is set aside **first**: 20% of the sales, stratified by price
quintile so that cheap and expensive houses are represented in both parts. It
is used **once**, at the end (@sec-housing-test).

```{python}
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet, Lasso, LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import (GridSearchCV, KFold, RepeatedKFold, cross_val_predict,
                                     cross_val_score, cross_validate, learning_curve, train_test_split)
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder, StandardScaler

houses = mlbook.load_housing()
NUMERIC = ["bedrooms", "bathrooms", "stories", "parking"]
BINARY = ["mainroad", "guestroom", "basement", "hotwaterheating", "airconditioning", "prefarea"]
FURNISHING = [["unfurnished", "semi-furnished", "furnished"]]

X = houses.drop(columns="price")
y_log = np.log(houses["price"])                         # a new name: re-running the cell changes nothing
price_band = pd.qcut(houses["price"], 5, labels=False)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y_log, test_size=0.2, stratify=price_band, random_state=42)
print(f"training {len(X_train)} sales, test {len(X_test)} sales (kept aside until the end)")
```

The data have no missing values (@sec-first-look), so nothing is deleted or
imputed for the analysis. The pipeline nevertheless includes median /
most-frequent **imputers**: a valuation engine will receive incomplete records,
and the imputers learn their fill values from the training data only. The
yes/no columns become 0/1; the furnishing status is one-hot encoded with
"unfurnished" as reference (its three levels are not equally spaced in their
effect, @sec-housing-sensitivity); every column is standardised so that the
penalties treat them alike (@sec-scaling). The lot area enters as its
**logarithm**, so that its coefficient is an elasticity like the target's
(@fig-simple-fit): this is the specification of the original study
[@anglin1996] and it fits slightly better (@sec-housing-sensitivity).

```{python}
def make_preprocessor(log_area=True, furnishing="onehot"):
    """Imputation, encoding and scaling, learned on the data passed to fit()."""
    area_steps = [("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"))]
    if log_area:
        area_steps.append(("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log, feature_names_out="one-to-one")))
    parts = [
        ("area", Pipeline(area_steps + [("scale", StandardScaler())]), ["area"]),
        ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), NUMERIC),
        ("bin", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                          ("encode", OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["no", "yes"]] * len(BINARY))),
                          ("scale", StandardScaler())]), BINARY)]
    if furnishing == "onehot":
        enc = OneHotEncoder(categories=FURNISHING, drop="first", sparse_output=False)
    elif furnishing == "ordinal":                                   # natural order
        enc = OrdinalEncoder(categories=FURNISHING)
    elif furnishing == "course codes":                              # furnished = 1, semi-furnished = 2
        enc = OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["unfurnished", "furnished", "semi-furnished"]])
    if furnishing != "none":
        parts.append(("furn", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")), ("encode", enc),
                                        ("scale", StandardScaler())]), ["furnishingstatus"]))
    return ColumnTransformer(parts, verbose_feature_names_out=False)

def model(regressor, **prep):
    return Pipeline([("prep", make_preprocessor(**prep)), ("reg", regressor)])

CV = RepeatedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=5, random_state=0)      # 25 fits per evaluation
FEATURES = make_preprocessor().fit(X_train).get_feature_names_out()
print(len(FEATURES), "features:", ", ".join(FEATURES))
```

### The baseline: is there overfitting? {#sec-housing-baseline}

```{python}
ols = model(LinearRegression())
cv_ols = cross_validate(ols, X_train, y_train, cv=CV, scoring=("neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"), return_train_score=True)
ols.fit(X_train, y_train)
baseline = pd.DataFrame({
    "MSE (log price)": [-cv_ols["train_neg_mean_squared_error"].mean(), -cv_ols["test_neg_mean_squared_error"].mean()],
    "R²": [cv_ols["train_r2"].mean(), cv_ols["test_r2"].mean()]},
    index=["fitted folds (training)", "held-out folds (validation)"])
print(baseline.round(4))
gap = baseline.iloc[1, 0] / baseline.iloc[0, 0] - 1
print(f"validation MSE exceeds training MSE by {100 * gap:.0f}%")
```

The validation error exceeds the training error by less than 10%, and the
$R^2$ drops by about three hundredths: the textbook signature of a model with
**little variance** (@tbl-diagnosis). With 13 coefficients and 436 training
sales — more than 30 sales per coefficient — and VIFs below 1.5
(@sec-multicollinearity), least squares has little room to overfit. The
learning curve confirms it:

```{python}
#| label: fig-housing-learning-curve
#| fig-cap: "Learning curve of the baseline (least squares on log-prices, repeated 5-fold CV). The two curves meet at a level well above zero: more data of the same kind would barely help; the remaining error is bias or noise, not variance."
sizes, tr, va = learning_curve(ols, X_train, y_train, cv=CV, train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1, 10),
                               scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
ax.plot(sizes, -tr.mean(1), marker="o", ms=4, label="training")
ax.plot(sizes, -va.mean(1), marker="o", ms=4, label="cross-validation")
ax.fill_between(sizes, -va.mean(1) - va.std(1) / 5, -va.mean(1) + va.std(1) / 5, color=mlbook.COLORS[1], alpha=0.2, lw=0)
ax.set_xlabel("training sales"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE of ln(price)"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The brief's hypothesis — overfitting — is **not supported** by the data.
Regularisation can still be compared, as requested, but we should not expect
it to reduce the error much (@thm-bias-variance: it trades variance, and there
is little variance to trade).

### Ridge, lasso and elastic net {#sec-housing-regularised}

Each model gets its own grid of 31 penalty values, wide enough to show the
whole curve: ridge from $10^{-2}$ to $10^4$; lasso from $\lambda_{\max}$
(@prp-lambda-max, computed on the training data) down to $10^{-4}\lambda_{\max}$;
elastic net with mixes 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 and a grid up to ten times
$\lambda_{\max}$ (its zero point is $\lambda_{\max}/\text{l1\_ratio}$). Every
candidate is scored by the same repeated 5-fold cross-validation, inside which
the whole pipeline is refitted.

```{python}
Z = make_preprocessor().fit_transform(X_train)
lam_max = np.max(np.abs(Z.T @ (y_train - y_train.mean()).to_numpy())) / len(y_train)
grids = {
    "ridge": (Ridge(), {"reg__alpha": np.logspace(-2, 4, 31)}),
    "lasso": (Lasso(max_iter=100_000), {"reg__alpha": lam_max * np.logspace(-4, 0, 31)}),
    "elastic net": (ElasticNet(max_iter=100_000), {"reg__alpha": lam_max * np.logspace(-4, 1, 31),
                                                   "reg__l1_ratio": [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]}),
}
searches = {name: GridSearchCV(model(est), grid, cv=CV, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error").fit(X_train, y_train)
            for name, (est, grid) in grids.items()}
print(f"lambda_max on the training data = {lam_max:.3f}")
for name, gs in searches.items():
    params = {k.replace("reg__", ""): round(float(v), 5) for k, v in gs.best_params_.items()}
    print(f"{name:12s} best {params}  CV MSE {-gs.best_score_:.4f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-housing-validation
#| fig-cap: "Error and sparsity as functions of the penalty (training data, repeated 5-fold CV). Top: cross-validated MSE of ln(price) ± 1 standard error; dashed: least squares. Bottom: number of non-zero coefficients of the model fitted on all training data. For the elastic net, the curve of the best mix is shown."
def curve(gs, l1=None):
    r = pd.DataFrame(gs.cv_results_)
    if l1 is not None:
        r = r[r["param_reg__l1_ratio"] == l1]
    alphas = r["param_reg__alpha"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return alphas, -r["mean_test_score"].to_numpy(), r["std_test_score"].to_numpy() / np.sqrt(CV.get_n_splits())

ols_cv_mse = -cv_ols["test_neg_mean_squared_error"].mean()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 4.8), sharex="col", gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 1]})
for col, (name, gs) in enumerate(searches.items()):
    l1 = gs.best_params_.get("reg__l1_ratio")
    alphas, mse, se = curve(gs, l1)
    c = mlbook.COLORS[col]
    axes[0, col].plot(alphas, mse, color=c); axes[0, col].fill_between(alphas, mse - se, mse + se, color=c, alpha=0.2, lw=0)
    axes[0, col].axhline(ols_cv_mse, color=mlbook.MUTED, ls="--", lw=1)
    axes[0, col].set_ylim(0.040, 0.075); axes[0, col].set_title(name + (f" (l1_ratio {l1})" if l1 else ""))
    est = grids[name][0]
    nz = [np.count_nonzero(model(est.set_params(alpha=a, **({"l1_ratio": l1} if l1 else {}))).fit(X_train, y_train)[-1].coef_)
          for a in alphas]
    axes[1, col].step(alphas, nz, where="mid", color=c)
    axes[1, col].set_xscale("log"); axes[1, col].set_xlabel("alpha (scikit-learn)"); axes[1, col].set_ylim(-0.5, 14)
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("CV MSE"); axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("non-zero")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The three curves have the same shape: flat — at the level of least squares —
until the penalty starts to remove real signal, then rising. The lasso keeps
all 13 coefficients throughout the flat region; it starts dropping features
only where the error is already increasing. Within one standard error of
the best score (@sec-selection), no model reaches a sparser solution:
**every characteristic carries some signal**.

### Comparing the models fairly {#sec-housing-comparison}

The best cross-validation scores above are optimistic (each is the best of
31–93 candidates, @sec-selection). For an honest comparison, **nested
cross-validation** repeats the whole tuning procedure inside each of 5 outer
folds; least squares, which has nothing to tune, is evaluated on the same outer
folds.

```{python}
outer = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)
inner = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=2)
candidates = {"least squares": model(LinearRegression())}
candidates |= {name: GridSearchCV(model(est), grid, cv=inner, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
               for name, (est, grid) in grids.items()}
rows = {}
for name, est in candidates.items():
    r = cross_validate(est, X_train, y_train, cv=outer, scoring=("neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"))
    mse = -r["test_neg_mean_squared_error"]
    est.fit(X_train, y_train)
    final = est.best_estimator_ if isinstance(est, GridSearchCV) else est
    rows[name] = {"MSE (log)": mse.mean(), "± s.e.": mse.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(mse)),
                  "RMSE (log)": np.sqrt(mse.mean()), "R²": r["test_r2"].mean(),
                  "non-zero coef.": np.count_nonzero(final[-1].coef_)}
comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
print(comparison.round(4).to_string())
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-housing-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Nested cross-validated MSE of ln(price) of the four models (mean over 5 outer folds, bars ±1 standard error; the horizontal axis does not start at zero). The differences between models are far smaller than the uncertainty of each estimate."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 2.6))
pos = np.arange(len(comparison))
ax.errorbar(comparison["MSE (log)"], pos, xerr=comparison["± s.e."], fmt="o", ms=8, color=mlbook.COLORS[0],
            ecolor=mlbook.INK2, capsize=4)
ax.set_yticks(pos, comparison.index); ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_ylim(len(pos) - 0.5, -0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("nested CV MSE of ln(price) (mean ± 1 s.e.)")
for p, v in zip(pos, comparison["MSE (log)"]):
    ax.annotate(f"{v:.4f}", (v, p), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, 8), ha="center", fontsize=8, color=mlbook.INK2)
plt.show()
```

The four models are indistinguishable: their errors differ in the fourth
decimal, while the standard error is in the third. In the units the brief
cares about, an RMSE of about 0.21 on log-prices means that a typical
valuation is off by roughly 20% of the price ($e^{0.21} \approx 1.23$ and
$e^{-0.21} \approx 0.81$).

### What drives the price: the coefficients {#sec-housing-coefficients}

All features are standardised, so the coefficients of the numerical features
are comparable with one another; those of the 0/1 features measure "having the
feature" in standard-deviation units of the indicator. The table shows the
four fitted models side by side, and the ratio $e^{b}$ as a percentage effect
on the price for a one-standard-deviation increase.

```{python}
fitted = {"least squares": model(LinearRegression()).fit(X_train, y_train)}
fitted |= {name: gs.best_estimator_ for name, gs in searches.items()}
coefs = pd.DataFrame({name: m[-1].coef_ for name, m in fitted.items()}, index=FEATURES)
coefs["% per s.d. (OLS)"] = 100 * (np.exp(coefs["least squares"]) - 1)
coefs = coefs.sort_values("least squares", key=np.abs, ascending=False)
print(coefs.round(3).to_string())
print("\nnon-zero:", {name: int(np.count_nonzero(m[-1].coef_)) for name, m in fitted.items()})
```

At their cross-validated penalties, the three regularised models are almost
indistinguishable from least squares: all keep the 13 coefficients, ridge
shrinks them all a little, lasso and elastic net barely touch them. The
difference between the methods shows along their **paths**
(@fig-reg-paths): increasing the penalty, ridge shrinks every coefficient
smoothly and never removes one, while the lasso removes them one by one. The
order in which the lasso keeps features as the penalty grows is a ranking of
their importance *given the others*:

```{python}
alphas = lam_max * np.logspace(0, -3, 300)
entered = {}
for a in alphas:
    c = model(Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=100_000)).fit(X_train, y_train)[-1].coef_
    for f in FEATURES[c != 0]:
        entered.setdefault(f, a / lam_max)
print("order in which features enter the lasso (alpha / lambda_max at entry):")
print(", ".join(f"{f} ({v:.2f})" for f, v in entered.items()))
```

The lot area enters first, then bathrooms, storeys and air conditioning,
then the preferred neighbourhood — the same features that dominate the
least-squares coefficients and the correlation matrix (@fig-corr-matrix); the
two furnishing indicators and the recreational room enter last. For explaining
valuations to clients, the honest statement is: *in this market, larger lots,
more storeys and bathrooms, central air conditioning, a furnished or
semi-furnished house, the preferred neighbourhood and a full basement are
associated with higher prices, other recorded characteristics being equal*; these are associations in 1987 Windsor sales,
not the effect of renovating a house (@sec-correlation).

### Test set and errors in price units {#sec-housing-test}

The test set is now used, once, for the four models. Errors are reported on
the log scale and in **price units**. Back-transforming a prediction of
$\ln y$ by $e^{\hat{\ln y}}$ estimates the *median* rather than the mean price
(the exponential of a mean of logs is a geometric mean); Duan's **smearing**
factor $\frac1n\sum_i e^{e_i}$, the average of the exponentiated training
residuals, corrects the bias without assuming normal errors [@duan1983].

```{python}
rows = {}
for name, m in fitted.items():
    pred_log = m.predict(X_test)
    smear = np.mean(np.exp(y_train - m.predict(X_train)))           # Duan's smearing factor, from training residuals
    price, pred_price = np.exp(y_test), np.exp(pred_log) * smear
    rows[name] = {"MSE (log)": mean_squared_error(y_test, pred_log), "R² (log)": r2_score(y_test, pred_log),
                  "RMSE (price)": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(price, pred_price)),
                  "MAE (price)": mean_absolute_error(price, pred_price),
                  "median |error| %": 100 * np.median(np.abs(pred_price - price) / price),
                  "smearing": smear}
test_results = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
print(test_results.round(4).to_string())
```

The test results agree with the cross-validation: the four models are
equivalent. The MSE on log-prices is about 0.04; in price units the RMSE is
about a million (the data set's prices are 1987 Canadian dollars multiplied by
70, so the absolute figures have no meaning for a client — the **relative**
error does): half of the test houses are valued within about 13% of their
sale price.

### Residuals: does the model err systematically? {#sec-housing-residuals}

Residuals are examined on **cross-validated predictions** of the training
data (each house predicted by a model that did not see it), so that the test
set stays untouched for the figures above.

```{python}
#| label: fig-housing-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals of the chosen model (ridge, cross-validated predictions on the training data). Left: residual against predicted ln(price). Centre: distribution of the residuals. Right: mean residual by quintile of the predicted price (blue) and of the actual price (orange); bars are ±1 standard error."
chosen = searches["ridge"].best_estimator_
cv_pred = cross_val_predict(chosen, X_train, y_train, cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0))
resid = y_train - cv_pred

def by_band(values):
    bands = pd.qcut(values, 5, labels=[f"Q{i}" for i in range(1, 6)])
    g = pd.Series(resid.to_numpy()).groupby(np.asarray(bands), observed=True)
    return g.mean(), g.std() / np.sqrt(g.size())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.2))
axes[0].scatter(cv_pred, resid, s=10, alpha=0.6, color=mlbook.COLORS[0]); axes[0].axhline(0, color=mlbook.INK2, lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("predicted ln(price)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("residual")
axes[1].hist(resid, bins=30, color=mlbook.COLORS[0], edgecolor="#fcfcfb"); axes[1].set_xlabel("residual")
for k, (label, values) in enumerate([("by predicted price", cv_pred), ("by actual price", y_train.to_numpy())]):
    m, s = by_band(values)
    axes[2].errorbar(np.arange(5) + (k - 0.5) * 0.18, m, yerr=s, fmt="o", color=mlbook.COLORS[k], label=label, capsize=3)
axes[2].axhline(0, color=mlbook.INK2, lw=1); axes[2].set_xticks(range(5), [f"Q{i}" for i in range(1, 6)])
axes[2].set_ylabel("mean residual"); axes[2].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"skewness of the residuals {pd.Series(resid).skew():.2f}; share of |residual| > 0.4: {np.mean(np.abs(resid) > 0.4):.1%}")
m_pred, _ = by_band(cv_pred); m_act, _ = by_band(y_train.to_numpy())
print("mean residual by predicted-price quintile:", m_pred.round(3).tolist())
print("mean residual by actual-price quintile:   ", m_act.round(3).tolist())
```

Against the **predicted** price the residuals are centred on zero in every
band: the model does not systematically over- or under-value houses that it
*predicts* to be cheap or expensive, and their spread is roughly constant
(the log scale removed the funnel shape that raw prices would show). Their
distribution is roughly symmetric (skewness close to zero), with a minority of
sales far from any prediction: 8% of residuals exceed 0.4 in absolute value,
i.e. the valuation is off by a factor of 1.5 or more.

Against the **actual** price, instead, the pattern is strong: cheap houses
are over-valued and expensive ones under-valued, by roughly 15–20% in the
lowest and highest quintiles. This is the answer to the brief's question "does the model err
systematically on the most expensive houses?" — yes, and it must be read
correctly, because part of it is a mathematical necessity, not a defect.

::: {#prp-residual-actual}
## Residuals always correlate with the actual value
For a least-squares fit with an intercept, on its training data, the
residuals are uncorrelated with the fitted values but have correlation
$\sqrt{1 - R^2}$ with the actual values.
:::

*In one line:* whenever the model explains only part of the price, the
houses that turned out most expensive are, on average, the ones it
under-predicted — regression towards the mean, again (@exr-ml4-regression-to-mean).

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-residual-actual
The residuals $e$ sum to zero and are orthogonal to the fitted values
(@thm-normal-equations), so $\sum_i e_i(\hat y_i - \bar y) = 0$: zero
correlation. With the actual values, $\sum_i e_i(y_i - \bar y) = \sum_i
e_i(\hat y_i - \bar y + e_i) = \sum_i e_i^2 = \mathrm{SSE}$, so the
correlation is $\mathrm{SSE}/\sqrt{\mathrm{SSE}\cdot\mathrm{SST}} =
\sqrt{\mathrm{SSE}/\mathrm{SST}} = \sqrt{1 - R^2}$. $\blacksquare$
:::

With $R^2 \approx 0.7$ the correlation is about 0.55, whatever the model: the
pattern by actual price measures how much of the price the features leave
unexplained. For the business it means that **for the most expensive
properties, the model's valuation will tend to be too low** (and for the
cheapest, too high): what makes them exceptional is precisely what the 12
recorded characteristics do not capture. Reducing it requires better
features (floor area, location, condition, date of sale), not regularisation.

### Sensitivity: the furnishing column and the lot area {#sec-housing-sensitivity}

The furnishing status has no documented origin (@sec-housing-data), and its
coding was a decision of the analysis. How much do the results depend on
these choices?

```{python}
variants = {
    "reference (log area, one-hot furnishing)": {},
    "area instead of log area": {"log_area": False},
    "furnishing ordinal, natural order": {"furnishing": "ordinal"},
    "furnishing ordinal, course codes (1, 2, 0)": {"furnishing": "course codes"},
    "without furnishing": {"furnishing": "none"},
}
sens = {}
for name, prep in variants.items():
    s = -cross_val_score(model(LinearRegression(), **prep), X_train, y_train, cv=CV, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
    sens[name] = {"CV MSE (log)": s.mean(), "± s.e.": s.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(s))}
print(pd.DataFrame(sens).T.round(4).to_string())
```

The logarithm of the lot area helps a little; one-hot encoding of the
furnishing status is the best of the codings — slightly better than the
natural-order ordinal coding, because semi-furnished and furnished houses have
almost the same coefficient relative to unfurnished ones (equal spacing is
the wrong assumption); the integer codes of the course's file, which happen to put
both furnished levels above unfurnished, do almost as well; dropping the
column costs about two standard errors. The undocumented column carries some signal, but the conclusions of the
analysis do not depend on it.

### Conclusions and recommendation {#sec-housing-conclusions}

Written as the closing text cell of the notebook, for readers who do not write
code:

> **What we did.** We compared four ways of estimating the sale price from
> twelve characteristics of a house: ordinary linear regression and its three
> regularised versions (ridge, lasso, elastic net). Every model was tuned and
> evaluated with the same repeated cross-validation on 80% of the sales, and
> checked once on the remaining 20%.
>
> **What we found.** (1) The current model does **not** overfit: its errors
> on unseen sales are only a few percent larger than on the sales it was
> fitted on, and adding data of the same kind would hardly help. (2)
> Consequently, regularisation does not improve accuracy: the four models
> make the same errors, to within the measurement uncertainty. (3) Half of the
> valuations are within about 13% of the sale price; about one in twelve is
> off by a factor of 1.5 or more. (4) The model undervalues the most
> expensive properties and overvalues the cheapest, by about 15–20% on average;
> this reflects what the twelve characteristics cannot see, not a technical
> error. (5) All twelve characteristics contribute; lot size, number of storeys,
> central air conditioning, bathrooms, furnishing and the preferred
> neighbourhood are the strongest *associations* with price.
>
> **Recommendation.** Keep a linear model on the logarithm of the price, with
> a light ridge penalty (it costs nothing in accuracy and protects against
> unstable coefficients if correlated features are added later), deployed as a
> single pipeline with the preprocessing. Report each valuation with its
> typical relative uncertainty (±20–25%). The larger errors on new properties
> are better explained by what the data do not contain — floor area, exact
> location, condition, and the date of the sale (these data are from 1987) —
> than by overfitting: improving the **data** is the next step, not tuning
> the penalty.

## Extensions {#sec-housing-extensions}

1. **Prediction intervals.** Report each valuation with an interval, using the
   empirical quantiles of the cross-validated residuals (on the log scale), and
   check its coverage on the test set.
2. **Non-linear effects.** Add interactions (for instance, bathrooms ×
   storeys) or splines of the log area, with ridge to control the extra
   variance; compare by nested cross-validation (@sec-polynomial).
3. **Market segments.** Cluster the houses as in @exr-ml7-houses and examine
   the residuals by segment; if segments are used as a feature, fit the
   clustering inside the pipeline (@sec-leakage).
4. **The original data.** Repeat the analysis on the 546 sales of the original
   study [@anglin1996data] without the undocumented furnishing column, and
   compare with the semiparametric results of Anglin and Gençay.
5. **A model card.** Document the final model — intended use, data, metrics,
   limitations (1987, one city, associations not effects) — following the
   "model cards" template [@mitchell2019].
6. **AI-assisted review.** Give an assistant the requirements of
   @sec-housing-brief and the original notebook with a structured prompt
   (@sec-structured-prompting), ask for a review, and compare its findings with
   @tbl-housing-review: did it notice the double logarithm without
   re-executing the notebook?

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- The companion notebook:
  [`Real_Estate_Price_Forecasting.ipynb`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-projects/blob/main/Real_Estate_Price_Forecasting.ipynb)
  (English) and its Italian original in the `it/` folder of
  [`ai-projects`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-projects).
- @anglin1996 — the original study of the Windsor data, comparing a parametric
  (Box–Cox, [@box1964]) and a semiparametric hedonic price model.
- @rosen1974 — the economic theory of hedonic prices: why regressing a price
  on characteristics makes sense, and what its coefficients mean.
- @duan1983 — predicting the mean of $y$ from a model of $\ln y$.
- @pimentel2019 — how often published notebooks fail to reproduce, and the
  practices that prevent it.
- @kapoor2023 — leakage and evaluation errors in applied machine learning, with
  a checklist that applies directly to projects like this one.
